summary: A Railway Technology feature by Eva Grey (March 7, 2016) reports on a study by the University of Cambridge, University of Minnesota and Minnesota State University Mankato, published September 2015 in Environmental Research Letters, finding that diesel train emissions at London Paddington station breach European nitrogen dioxide limits and exceed nearby roadside levels. The article places this in the context of rail's overall low emissions share, EU and UK regulation, emissions-reduction targets, and alternatives such as battery trains and retrofitted diesel engines. Much of the page is navigation, GlobalData marketing and a sample-download form, which were ignored.
one_line: A 2016 Railway Technology feature on study findings that diesel train emissions at London Paddington station exceed European air quality limits.
key_facts: The study on diesel train emissions at London Paddington station was published in September 2015 in the journal Environmental Research Letters.
Researchers from the University of Cambridge, University of Minnesota and Minnesota State University Mankato conducted the study.
Air quality at London Paddington train station was evaluated over a period of five days and was found in breach of European limits for nitrogen dioxide (NO2) each time.
Paddington station serves 38 million passengers annually, making it the seventh busiest station in the UK.
Up to 70% of trains passing through Paddington station are powered by diesel engines.
Eight million passengers pass through UK railway stations every day, and UK stations are not required to comply with EU air quality standards.
British rolling stock has a mean age of 18 years.

Rail accounted for 0.8% of transport sector emissions between 1990 and 2009, while the entire transport sector contributes about 22% of global emissions, according to European Environment Agency (EEA) statistics.
Public Health England estimates that 29,000 deaths a year in the UK are caused by air pollution.
About 20% of Europe's current rail traffic is hauled by diesel locomotives, according to the European Commission.
In the EEA-33 area, 53% of the rail network was electrified by 2013, while only 41% of UK train tracks are electrified.

In December 2015, the International Union of Railways' Low Carbon Sustainable Rail Transport Challenge aimed for 50% cuts in energy consumption and CO2 emissions from train operations by 2030 relative to 1990, and a 60% total energy reduction by 2050.
The Clean European Rail-Diesel (CleanER-D) project, led by the European Railway Industry Association, dedicated £8.9m between 2009 and 2013 and ended in January 2014.

The Independently Powered Electric Multiple Unit (IPEMU) was the first battery-powered train to start service on the UK rail network after more than 50 years, running between Harwich International and Manningtree stations in Essex.
The £2.8bn upgrade of the Great Western mainline from London to Cardiff was pushed back from an initial 2018 deadline to 2020.
